Q: "Debug" function in Chrome A:

This is documented in the Console Utilities API Reference:

debug(function)

When the specified function is called, the debugger is invoked and breaks inside the function on the Sources panel allowing to step through the code and debug it.

debug(getData);

Use undebug(fn) to stop breaking on the function, or use the UI to disable all breakpoints.

For more information on breakpoints, see Pause Your Code With Breakpoints.

Q: Is there a non-atomic equivalent of std::shared_ptr? And why isn't there one in <memory>? A:

Well, you hit std::shared_ptr nail on its head:

  • std::shared_ptr always atomic reference counter increments/decrements are rather undesirable premature pessimisation, by definition.
  • std::shared_ptr comprised of 2 pointer members is the most wasteful shared pointer implementation.
  • Whether the object reference counter is atomic or not is a property of the class of an object, rather than pointer type std::shared_ptr<T> vs std::local_shared_ptr<T>.
  • Having to change all existing declaration from std::shared_ptr<T> to std::local_shared_ptr<T> or vice versa when changing the class-specific reference counter type is rather undesirable and unacceptable.
  • std::enable_shared_from_this would be the right place/hook to specify the type/atomicity of the reference counter.

std::shared_ptr<T> is a universally robust smart-pointer with shared-ownership.

However, any code using std::shared_ptr<T> is a universally organically grown hair-ball of application components, which gets difficult to maintain and evolve over time. That often manifests in extra T::init/T::deinit functions that must be called in addition to constructors/destructors to break any cyclic references established by std::shared_ptr<T> members. Ends in tears, obviously.

Spotting std::shared_ptr<T> usage in a codebase begs for redesigning the application to establish a clear hierarchy of component lifetimes and object ownership in such a way that no shared/unclear ownership is ever needed.

One pretty much never wants to use std::shared_ptr<T>. Unless std::weak_ptr<T> is needed, which is a work-around for preventing std::shared_ptr<T> cyclic references.

The briefly mentioned boost::intrusive_ptr should be the default smart-pointer type for objects with shared ownership because:

  • boost::intrusive_ptr<T> invokes class T specific reference counter increment/decrement functions. Modifying the reference counter type in class T to be atomic or not, doesn't require modifying the source code of all its boost::intrusive_ptr<T> users.
  • boost::intrusive_ptr<T> comprised of 1 pointer member is 0-waste -- smart pointers don't get any more space-efficient than that.
  • Class T embeds the reference counter, hence declaring how its lifetime is managed. This allows passing around references to T objects as T* or T& (and never by value T), and sharing the object only where necessary by constructing a boost::intrusive_ptr<T> from T* or T& on the spot by passing them to boost::intrusive_ptr<T> ptr(T*)/ptr(T&) factory function overloads.
  • Passing around references to T objects as T* or T& prevents undesirable pollution of interfaces with specific smart-pointer types.

Shared pointers are solutions that prevent shared objects from being destroyed prematurely. std::shared_ptr is the most expensive shared pointer type.

A pure 0-cost solution to this problem is establishing application component hierarchy and lifetimes in such a way, that components are created and destroyed in the fixed nesting order established by the source code. So that lower level components refer their higher level ones using plain T* only -- because the lifetime of the higher level components includes that of the lower level ones by source code definition/construction order.

This still may require passing object (message) ownership from a lower level to a higher, or vice versa, or between threads through message queues -- std::unique_ptr is the ideal 0-overhead solution.

In summary:

  • Whether ownership of an object is supposed be shared or not is a property of the object's class only.
  • Embedding the reference counter into the object allows the full control of its update atomicity, in one place -- its class definition.
  • Polluting function interfaces with specific smart-pointer parameters is an anti-pattern. While factory functions must return specific smart-pointer types when transferring ownership to the caller, of course.
  • std::shared_ptr<T> is the ideal smart-pointer for textbooks. It should never be used in production code, though.
  • std::unique_ptr<T> is the ideal choice for transferring object ownership.
  • boost::intrusive_ptr<T> is the ideal default choice when shared object ownership is desired.

Q: JPA Logging Level on Glassfish v3 Server A:

Long answer for Sorro's comment

With the following setup you can change log level in Payara Micro on the fly without restart by help of property enableDynamicLogging. Payara Server should be similar. Setup also respects EclipseLink parameter and transaction logging.

persistence.xml

<persistence version="3.0" xmlns="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:schemaLocation="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence/persistence_3_0.xsd">
  <persistence-unit
    name="db"
    transaction-type="JTA">
    <jta-data-source>java:global/datasource</jta-data-source>
    <properties>
      <property name="eclipselink.logging.parameters" value="true"/>
    </properties>
  </persistence-unit>
</persistence>

This is much less config than said in https://wiki.eclipse.org/EclipseLink/Examples/JPA/Logging or any other Internet source you find. Hence EclipseLink log level properties and property eclipselink.logging.logger is not needed. You can use the same persistence.xml in Arquillian.

logging.properties

handlers=java.util.logging.ConsoleHandler
java.util.logging.ConsoleHandler.formatter=com.sun.enterprise.server.logging.ODLLogFormatter
com.sun.enterprise.server.logging.ODLLogFormatter.ansiColor=true
java.util.logging.ConsoleHandler.level=INFO

org.eclipse.persistence.level=FINER
my.package=FINER

This is Payara default logging.properties appended by EclipseLink and own code stuff.

build.gradle

...
def loggingProperties = layout.projectDirectory.file("logging.properties").asFile.path

test {
    ...
    systemProperty("java.util.logging.config.file", loggingProperties)
}

payaraMicro {
    environment 'payaramicro_logPropertiesFile':loggingProperties,
            'payaramicro_enableDynamicLogging':true
    ...
}
...

Other build tools analogous.

Dockerfile

FROM payara/micro:6.2025.7-jdk21

ARG LOGGING_PROPERTIES="logging.properties"

WORKDIR $DEPLOY_DIR
COPY --chmod=644 build/libs/app-*.war .
COPY --chmod=644 $LOGGING_PROPERTIES .
RUN sed -i 's/\r$//' $LOGGING_PROPERTIES
RUN ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sed -i -e 's/.level=INFO/.level=${ENV=LOG_LEVEL}/g' $LOGGING_PROPERTIES"]

WORKDIR /opt/payara

ENV payaramicro_logPropertiesFile=$DEPLOY_DIR/$LOGGING_PROPERTIES
ENV payaramicro_enableDynamicLogging=true

Having ENV stuff by default in logging.properties can not be handled by gradle test task. The ENV value is taken from docker compose env file and can not be changed without upping again. Hence if you want to change log level in container on the fly define log level directly in logging.properties in container.

Payara supports some kind of relaxed binding like Spring. Meaning Java System Property names are mapped to environment variables names.

Q: ggplot in a for-loop with varying x-values A:

The issue is caused by lazy evaluation inside aes().

In your loop, aes(x = m, y = V1) does not immediately lock m as "V2", "V3", etc. The plot object keeps a reference to m, and when the plots are printed later, m has already ended as "V4". So all plots end up using the final loop value.

Use tidy evaluation to force the column name at plot creation time.

library(tidyverse)

df <- data.frame(
  "V1" = c(0, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50),
  "V2" = c(0, 1, 3, 6, 9, 18, 53),
  "V3" = c(0, 0.5, 1.2, 3, 7, 9, 27),
  "V4" = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0)
)

measured <- colnames(df[2:ncol(df)])
plots_cali <- list()

for (m in measured) {
  
  namx <- paste("Measured concentration of ", m, " in g/l", sep = "")
  namy <- paste("Ideal concentration of ", m, " in g/l", sep = "")
  
  plots_cali[[m]] <- ggplot(df, aes(x = !!sym(m), y = V1)) +
    labs(x = namx, y = namy) +
    geom_smooth(
      method = "lm",
      se = TRUE,
      color = "#1E88E5",
      fill = "#90CAF9"
    ) +
    geom_point()
}

plots_cali[["V2"]]
plots_cali[["V3"]]
plots_cali[["V4"]]

The key change is aes(x = m, y = V1) -> aes(x = !!sym(m), y = V1)

  1. sym(m) converts the string "V2" into the column symbol V2.

  2. !! injects that symbol into aes() immediately.

  3. So each plot stores the correct column: V2, V3, or V4.

Q: Is switching from C++ to Python for DSA a good decision? A:

A stack is a stack no matter the language... except you will never ever "implement" a stack in python. You'll just use the already-existing list type with its append and pop methods.

Python is a fun language to manipulate stuff fast, but it's not a language anyone uses to reinvent the wheel.

  • If the goal is to learn data structures by reimplementing them from scratch, then that goal is not going to be achieved in python.
  • If the goal is to learn data structures by using them to solve problems, then sure, python is a great language for that.

Q: Handling log inconsistencies in Raft: how should a follower reconcile conflicting entries? A:

One question I have is: is it possible for a follower to have a conflicting log like this?

1: A, 2: X, 3: C

Could this desync happen due to a leader crash or other failures?

No. A follower should not be able to enter this state.

Entry 3 could only have been appended after entry 2 already existed.

Suppose the leader originally created:

1:A
2:B
3:C

When it sent entry 3, it also sent:

prevLogIndex = 2
prevLogTerm = term(B)

The follower would only accept entry 3 if its own entry at index 2 matched the leader's term.

If it instead had

2:X

(with a different term), it would reject the AppendEntries RPC.

So the follower can never end up with

1:A
2:X
3:C

Assuming this is possible, how should the follower reconcile its log with the leader’s?

We can't assume the protocol to recover from a state that it can't enter by design.

A possible case that shows how the protocol works, would be i.e.

  1. Old leader creates X, Y, Z.

  2. Old leader crashes before they're committed.

  3. A different server becomes leader.

  4. New leader has C, D instead.

So we end up with this

Leader:

1:A
2:B
3:C
4:D

Follower:

1:A
2:B
3:X
4:Y
5:Z

This is where prevLogIndex and prevLogTerm come in.

Suppose the leader wants to replicate D.

It sends

AppendEntries
prevLogIndex = 3
prevLogTerm  = term(C)

entries = [4:D]

Follower checks:

my entry at index 3

It finds

3:X

whose term is different.

It replies:

Failure

Nothing changes yet.

The leader also maintains a nextIndex for every follower.

Failure means:

"You're assuming I match through index 4. I don't."

The leader decreases nextIndex.

Now it retries with

prevLogIndex = 2
prevLogTerm = term(B)

entries =
3:C
4:D

Now the follower checks:

index 2

It matches.

At this point Raft does something important:

Delete everything after index 2.

So

1:A
2:B
3:X
4:Y
5:Z

becomes

1:A
2:B

Then it appends

3:C
4:D

Result:

1:A
2:B
3:C
4:D

Now the logs match perfectly.

If a follower wanted to commit its entries in this scenario, would it need to compare every log entry one by one with the leader’s log? That seems very expensive and inefficient. How does Raft efficiently handle this kind of inconsistency without checking each entry individually every time?

Suppose the follower is far behind. The leader might try:

index 100
fail

99
fail

98
fail

97
fail
...

The original Raft paper describes exactly this simple algorithm, but it also mentions an optimization.

Modern implementations typically have the follower return additional information like:

  • the conflicting term

  • the first index where that term appears

Instead of backing up one entry at a time, the leader can jump over entire ranges of conflicting entries.

This makes recovery much faster when logs have diverged significantly.

Q: MySQL SELECT query with ORDER BY and LIMIT then use ORDER BY on the limited rows A:

Try this:

SELECT * FROM table WHERE id IN (
   SELECT ID FROM table ORDER BY ID ASC LIMIT 0, 1000
) ORDER BY name ASC

As mentioned in comments that subquery is not supported, 'This version of MySQL doesn't yet support 'LIMIT & IN/ALL/ANY/SOME subquery'. Using JOINs is the only alternative left, like this:

SELECT table.* FROM tab JOIN (
   SELECT ID FROM table ORDER BY ID LIMIT 1000
) temp
ON table.ID = temp.ID
ORDER BY table.name
